speaker: Amrit Venkatesh, University of Virginia

Solid-state NMR spectroscopy is uniquely suited to probe local structure and dynamics in complex materials, but its application is often constrained by inherently low sensitivity. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Atomic-Level Characterization of Materials using Advanced Solid-State NMR Abstract : Establishing atomic-level structure-property relationships is essential for understanding and designing functional materials. Solid-state NMR spectroscopy is uniquely suited to probe local structure and dynamics in complex materials, but its application is often constrained by inherently low sensitivity. The Venkatesh group develops and applies dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) and fast magic-angle spinning (MAS) methods that dramatically enhance the sensitivity and resolution of solid-state NMR experiments. These advances enable high-resolution studies of nuclei across the Periodic Table and facilitate multidimensional investigations of heterogeneous materials, including surfaces, interfaces, and nanostructured systems. In this seminar, we will highlight recent efforts to characterize complex materials relevant to catalysis and energy, demonstrating how advanced solid-state NMR methodologies provide atomic-level insights that are inaccessible by conventional approaches. Bio : Dr. Amrit Venkatesh is an Assistant Professor of Chemistry at the University of Virginia (UVA), where he leads a research program focused on developing dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) enhanced and advanced solid-state NMR methods for characterizing complex materials. He received his Ph.D. in Chemistry from Iowa State University, earning the Zaffarano Award in 2021 for outstanding doctoral research. He subsequently held a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral Fellowship at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Switzerland, and later served as Research Faculty at the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory at Florida State University. At UVA, his research combines methodological innovation in magnetic resonance with applications to heterogeneous materials, surfaces, catalysts, and energy-relevant systems, with the goal of establishing atomic-level structure-property relationships that guide materials design.

speaker: Yuriy Roman, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
content: Reimagining Thermochemical Catalysis: Promoting Reactions with Electric FieldsAbstract: Catalysis has long relied on conventional handles such as temperature, pressure, and concentration to accelerate chemical reactions. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Reimagining Thermochemical Catalysis: Promoting Reactions with Electric Fields Abstract : Catalysis has long relied on conventional handles such as temperature, pressure, and concentration to accelerate chemical reactions. Across biology and electrochemistry, electric fields provide an additional parameter to control rates. Enzymes exploit strong, oriented fields within their active sites to stabilize intermediates and accelerate turnover, while in electrochemistry, interfacial polarization dictates electron and proton transfer rates. In heterogeneous thermochemical catalysis, however, little is known about these effects, yet they may offer new opportunities to control reactivity. In this talk, I will describe our group’s efforts to harness electric fields to promote thermochemical reactions. For many electrochemical half-reactions, varying the applied potential accelerates rates by driving rate-controlling proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) steps. We hypothesized that if an elementary PCET step were embedded within a thermochemical reaction, its strong potential dependence could be leveraged to enhance the overall rate. Because interfacial PCET involves proton exchange across the electric double layer, we anticipated that Brønsted acid catalysis, governed by proton transfer, would be particularly susceptible to polarization. First, I will show how spontaneous interfacial fields at conductive particles dispersed in liquid media can measurably modulate turnover rates. Next, I will discuss how applied potentials produce reversible, exponential rate promotion in acid-catalyzed alcohol dehydration, accelerating rates by up to five orders of magnitude while the overall catalytic cycle remains non-Faradaic. Our kinetic analyses reveal that this acceleration arises from a field-driven increase in the population of reactive intermediates prior to the rate-determining step, providing a mechanistic basis for log-linear rate scaling with potential. I will then examine how electrolyte concentration and solvent properties set the interfacial potential profile and the fraction of the potential drop sampled by proton transfer, which separates electrostatic promotion from conventional solvent effects. In highly polar solvents, even trace ionic species can place nominally electrolyte-free reactions in a strongly suppressed regime through the catalyst's native open-circuit potential. Finally, I will highlight our development of polarized slurry reactors, which extend these principles from 2D electrodes to 3D catalyst slurries and enable rate enhancements under conditions more suitable for scale-up. These results establish interfacial electric fields and catalyst potential as design variables for controlling thermochemical reactivity and developing scalable catalytic processes. Bio : Yuriy Román-Leshkov is the Robert T. Haslam Professor of Chemical Engineering at MIT, where he joined the faculty in 2010 and holds a joint appointment in the Department of Chemistry. His research group works at the intersection of heterogeneous catalysis, materials science, and sustainable chemical processes. His research group designs heterogeneous catalysts and functional materials to tackle sustainability challenges in energy and chemicals. His group pioneered the use of electric fields to promote thermochemical reactions, developed catalytic routes to convert lignin into drop-in sustainable aviation fuel components, established the analytical and reactor engineering foundations for the chemical recycling of polyolefins, and created data-driven tools to predict zeolite synthesis. Several of these technologies are on a path to commercialization. Together, these efforts build the foundation for a circular, low-carbon chemical industry. From 2023 to 2025 he served as Chief Scientist of Solugen, where he led catalyst development for the production of bio-based chemicals at the ton scale. A native of Mexico City, he earned his B.S. at the University of Pennsylvania and his Ph.D. at the University of Wisconsin-Madison under the supervision of Prof. Jim Dumesic, followed by postdoctoral research at Caltech under the guidance of Prof. Mark Davis. He has authored more than 200 peer-reviewed articles and holds 28 patents. His work has been recognized with the Paul H. Emmett Award in Fundamental Catalysis, the International Catalysis Award from the International Association of Catalysis Societies, the NSF CAREER Award, the ACS Early Career in Catalysis Award, the AIChE Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division Young Investigator Award, among other honors.

speaker: Alan West, Columbia University
content: Critical Materials Processing via Closed-Loop Redox-Mediated LeachingAbstract: Electrification can transform the way chemical reagents are produced, regenerated, and integrated into industrial processes. In hydrometallurgy, electrochemical regeneration of redox carriers enables closed-loop redox-mediated leaching (CL-RML), changing the relationship between reagent selection, process performance, and sustainability. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Critical Materials Processing via Closed-Loop Redox-Mediated Leaching Abstract: Electrification can transform the way chemical reagents are produced, regenerated, and integrated into industrial processes. In hydrometallurgy, electrochemical regeneration of redox carriers enables closed-loop redox-mediated leaching (CL-RML), changing the relationship between reagent selection, process performance, and sustainability. Rather than treating oxidants or reductants as consumable reagents, CL-RML allows redox carriers to be selected primarily for their extraction performance and selectivity. This seminar will discuss a framework of closed-loop redox chemistry and discuss how it expands the design space for critical-materials extraction. Recent studies of nickel and copper extraction from sulfide minerals will be presented to illustrate how electrochemically regenerated redox carriers enable new opportunities to control mineral transformations, improve selectivity, and rethink process architecture. These examples demonstrate how regeneration influences not only leaching chemistry, but also upstream and downstream processes. By leveraging scalable industrial electrochemical technologies, closed-loop redox chemistry offers a pathway toward more modular, flexible extraction processes capable of treating increasingly complex mineral resources. Together, these concepts suggest that the greatest opportunity of CL-RML may be to expand the chemical and process design space available for future critical-minerals supply chains while simultaneously improving sustainability. Bio: Alan West is the Samuel Ruben–Peter G. Viele Professor of Electrochemistry at Columbia University, with appointments in the Department of Chemical Engineering, the Department of Earth and Environmental Engineering, and the Columbia Climate School. He is also Co-Director of the Columbia Electrochemical Energy Center, which has grown to 14 core faculty from five departments. Professor West received his B.S. in Chemical Engineering from Case Western Reserve University and his Ph.D. in Chemical Engineering from the University of California, Berkeley. His research integrates electrochemistry, reaction engineering, and hydrometallurgy to develop sustainable technologies for critical materials production, resource recovery, batteries, electrochemical synthesis, and electrodeposition. His recent work focuses on electrochemically regenerated redox carriers and closed-loop redox-mediated leaching for the selective extraction of critical metals from sulfide minerals and other complex resources.Professor West previously served as Chair of Columbia's Department of Chemical Engineering for eight years, during a period of significant growth and expansion. He is a Fellow of The Electrochemical Society.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Creating Abundance through Catalysis Abstract : Humanity is at a crossroads trying to drive future advancements in science and quality of life with significant challenges related to global climate change, economic insecurity, and natural resource constraints. The evolution of the energy landscape is one challenge that must be addressed to ensure that we continue to thrive. The centralized model to power generation is starting to fray; and whether that’s related to supporting the rising need for data storage, electrification for mobility or the technologies needed to combat climate change, a decentralized model needs to grow to replace it. This model creates new challenges with regards to emissions and efficiency, but potentially creates opportunities for new technologies and new fuels often driven by catalysis. Johnson Matthey’s Clean Air Solutions team has been supporting a diverse range of industries from data centers to coal mines through these challenges leveraging our core competencies of platinum group metal refining and emission control as well as our growing strengths in fuel cells, carbon capture and methane removal. Here we will discuss some of those challenges and how as scientists we identify markets, partners and potential products, creating opportunities for ourselves as well as the partners we support. We will discuss some of the pitfalls product designers can face and share our insights into where new developments can make a meaningful difference toward designing a bright future. Bio : Joseph Fedeyko is currently the Business Development Manager for Johnson Matthey’s Clean Air Solutions Team. He holds a Ph. D. in Chemical Engineering from the University of Delaware. Since joining Johnson Matthey in 2006, he has been the driving force for innovative technologies across catalysis, material development, process development, and system design, resulting in 50 granted patent families and significant product launches. In addition, he has dedicated his time to serving in several leadership roles in both the Catalysis Club of Philadelphia and the North-East Corridor Zeolite Association. His current role coordinates product development, engineering, sales and business development for existing stationary emission markets and the development of new market opportunities to support decarbonization and the energy transition.

speaker: Dimitris Lagoudas, Texas A&M University

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Recent Advances in the Modeling of Shape Memory Alloys Abstract : Shape memory alloys (SMAs) exhibit unique behavior due to reversible phase transformations that are strongly influenced by material composition, microstructure, and applied thermal and mechanical loads. Under complex loading conditions, including simultaneous and out-of-phase thermal and mechanical loading, SMAs can show transformation behavior that differs from that observed in traditional experiments. These observations highlight the need to better connect material behavior at the microscale with the overall response of the material. Micromechanics modeling provides a framework for connecting SMA microstructures to macroscopic thermomechanical behavior. At the same time, advances in additive manufacturing make it possible to control microstructures within a single material system, creating new opportunities to study how processing parameters influence SMA properties. Because there are many possible processing and composition combinations, modeling can help predict complex material behavior of phase transforming materials and reduce the number of experiments needed to fully characterize their behavior. This presentation will discuss how physics-based multiscale modeling combined with data-driven approaches can be used to model the thermomechanical constitutive response of high temperature SMAs and identify compositions and processing parameters that meet specific performance requirements. It will also examine the opportunities and limitations of combining experiments, thermodynamic modeling, and data-driven methods to more efficiently and accurately predict the complex behavior of high temperature SMA materials. Bio : Dimitris C. Lagoudas is a University Distinguished Professor, Regents Professor, Robert C. “Bud” Hagner Chair of Engineering, and Head of the Department of Aerospace Engineering at Texas A&M University. A nationally recognized leader in engineering research and administration, he has held numerous senior leadership positions across the university and The Texas A&M University System, including Senior Associate Vice Chancellor for Research, Associate Vice President for Research, Senior Associate Dean for Research, Deputy Director of the Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station (TEES), and Director of two TEES research centers. Throughout his distinguished career, Dr. Lagoudas has served both as interim and permanent Head of the Department of Aerospace Engineering and as the inaugural Chair of Texas A&M University's Materials Science and Engineering graduate program. His leadership has contributed significantly to advancing research, innovation, and interdisciplinary collaboration across engineering and the broader academic community. D.C. Lagoudas’ research involves the design, characterization and modeling of multifunctional materials at multiple scales, with advanced averaging micromechanics methods developed to bridge the various length scales and functionalities, including mechanical, thermal and electrical. His research team is recognized internationally for modeling and characterization of shape memory alloys. He has co-authored more than 600 scientific publications in archival journals and conference proceedings and one of the most widely used books on shape memory alloys. D.C. Lagoudas received the 2006 ASME Adaptive Structures and Material Systems Prize in recognition of his contributions to the modeling and characterization of shape memory alloys and their use in aerospace structures and he is the 2011 recipient of the Smart Structure and Materials Lifetime Achievement Award. A Fellow of AIAA, ASME, and SES, Lagoudas was named a University Distinguished Professor at Texas A&M University in 2013 and a Regents Professor of the Texas A&M University System in 2025. In 2026, he received the SES Yonggang Huang Engineering Science Medal.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Beyond Conventional Silicon: Perovskite Solar Cells and X-ray Detectors Abstract : Silicon underpins modern electronics, yet its technological dominance and geographically concentrated supply chains present growing concerns. In this talk, I will introduce halide perovskites, a class of high-performance semiconductors that can be synthesized and processed at relatively simple conditions. I will describe our progress in scalable perovskite solar cells fabricated in ambient air using green solvents, followed by the automated growth of single crystals for emerging X-ray photon-counting medical imaging. These examples will illustrate how solution chemistry and automation can enable new semiconductors beyond conventional silicon. Bio: Makhsud Saidaminov is a Canada Research Chair in Advanced Functional Materials and Associate Professor at the University of Victoria. His research focuses on solution-processed materials and their applications, guided by the vision that technologies should not be luxuries but broadly accessible. Raised in Tajikistan, he received his PhD from Lomonosov Moscow State University and held postdoctoral fellowships at KAUST and the University of Toronto. He has been recognized as a Highly Cited Researcher since 2021, received the Canadian Society for Chemistry’s Keith Laidler Award, and serves as an Associate Editor of ACS Photonics. He is also a co-founder of AY Sensors, which develops perovskite X-ray photon-counting detectors for medical imaging.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Atomically Thin Membranes: Opportunities and Challenges Abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) nanomaterials offer fundamentally new opportunities to study mass transport at sub-atomic and molecular length scales. Their atomic thickness enables transport phenomena such as quantum tunneling, while their ability to host atomically precise defects that function as nanopores enables highly size-selective ionic and molecular sieving. Together, these unique characteristics open new frontiers in membrane science and molecular separations. In this talk, I will discuss our recent advances in the synthesis, fundamental transport characterization, scalable processing, and device integration of 2D materials. I will highlight their application as next-generation proton exchange membranes for fuel cells and redox flow batteries, where atomically thin selective layers can overcome the long-standing permeability–selectivity trade-off that limits conventional membrane technologies. Finally, I will present emerging opportunities for 2D materials to enable entirely new separation processes, including highly energy-efficient hydrogen isotope separation. Bio : Piran R. Kidambi is an Associate Professor at the University of Florida. After receiving his PhD from the University of Cambridge, he pursued postdoctoral research at MIT through a Lindemann Trust Fellowship. Kidambi's research leverages the intersection between (i) nanomaterial synthesis, (ii) process engineering, and (iii) in situ metrology, to enable bottom-up materials design and synthesis for energy, separations, and healthcare applications. His research has been recognized via several awards and honors. Related documents Atomically Thin Membranes
